clinicalPearls: One of the commoner enzyme defects of red-cell nucleotide metabolism, causing chronic non-spherocytic, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia
The blood film hallmark is prominent coarse basophilic stippling, an unusual finding for an inherited haemolytic anaemia
Because lead inhibits this same enzyme, the picture closely mimics lead poisoning and the two must be distinguished
Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, so consanguinity or affected siblings may be present
Retained pyrimidine nucleotides accumulate in the red cell and can be detected as an abnormal nucleotide profile
Diagnosis rests on reduced enzyme activity on assay together with the characteristic stippling and NT5C3A mutation testing
Management is supportive with folate and transfusion when needed; the anaemia is usually mild to moderate and splenectomy gives limited benefit
reference.pathophysiology: Pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase dephosphorylates pyrimidine nucleotides during the degradation of RNA as reticulocytes mature, allowing the breakdown products to leave the cell. When the enzyme is deficient, pyrimidine nucleotides accumulate within the red cell, aggregate with ribosomal remnants to produce the coarse basophilic stippling seen on the film, and disturb nucleotide balance and glycolytic metabolism, shortening cell survival and causing a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. Because lead directly inhibits the enzyme, lead intoxication reproduces the same biochemical and morphological picture.
additionalDifferentials: Thalassaemia and other causes of basophilic stippling
additionalInvestigations: Blood film examination for coarse basophilic stippling
Blood lead concentration to exclude lead poisoning
Red-cell nucleotide profile showing pyrimidine accumulation
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Molecular testing of the NT5C3A gene
redFlags: Failure to exclude lead poisoning, which is treatable and potentially serious
Aplastic crisis after parvovirus B19 infection
Transfusional iron overload in more severe disease
reference.prognosis: The anaemia is typically mild to moderate and lifelong but well tolerated, with a generally good prognosis once lead poisoning has been excluded.
pitfalls: Failing to check a blood lead level and missing treatable lead intoxication that mimics the disorder
Attributing basophilic stippling to thalassaemia without considering an enzyme defect
Expecting splenectomy to substantially improve the anaemia
Overlooking the abnormal red-cell nucleotide profile that supports the diagnosis
